facts.name: Oath Wallet
facts.platform: iPhone and iPad; Apple App Store
facts.price: Free to download. Review the network fee in Oath before sending. A sending exchange or other service may charge a separate fee.
facts.address: 2103 Condor Ct, Redmond, Oregon 97756-8281, United States
facts.custody: Oath never holds, controls or has access to user funds, private keys, recovery phrases or passkeys. It cannot recover, reverse or freeze transactions.
facts.account: No account, email, phone number or KYC is required to use Oath.
facts.confirm: Transactions are authorized after reviewing the amount, destination, network and estimated fee. The final network fee and confirmation depend on the chain.

features.name: Check and revoke token approvals
features.summary: Check discovered token approvals in Oath for iPhone. Review supported EVM, TRON and Solana access, estimate network fees and verify supported revocations.

scope.label: EVM networks
scope.detail: Supported token allowances, NFT approvals and Permit2 operations. Review the exact permission and network; not every contract or account-control entry can be removed.

scope.label: TRON
scope.detail: Supported token and collectible permissions use the TRON removal flow. Account-control keys have a different scope and are not ordinary token allowances.

scope.label: Solana
scope.detail: Supported token-account delegate revocations. Permanent delegates and other token restrictions are not interchangeable with removable account delegates.

features.limitations: The released app can discover and prepare supported removals on these network families. Coverage depends on providers, the account and the permission type.
steps: Open Settings → Permissions → Token access. Wait for the scan and read its coverage status.
Match the network, asset and approved address. Open a removable entry and review what the removal will change.
Check the fee, confirm in Oath and follow Recent changes. Refresh the scan after confirmation before treating access as removed.

questions.q: Does disconnecting a dApp revoke its token approvals?
questions.a: No. A WalletConnect session and an on-chain allowance are different permissions. Disconnect the session when needed, and review token access separately.

questions.q: Does an empty scan mean my wallet has no approvals?
questions.a: No. Read whether coverage is checked, partial, unavailable or unsupported. An unavailable provider or incomplete discovery must not be treated as proof that no permissions exist.

questions.q: Can revoking an approval recover stolen funds?
questions.a: No. Revocation can remove supported future access after it is confirmed; it does not reverse completed transfers or cancel every possible off-chain signature.

questions.q: Do I need a network fee balance?
questions.a: Yes, supported revocations require the relevant network fee asset. Review the actual estimate in Oath before confirming.

features.name: Encrypted iCloud wallet backup
features.summary: Back up eligible Oath wallets to iCloud Drive with password encryption. Learn what is supported, how to confirm uploads and what you need to restore.

scope.label: Eligible active wallets
scope.detail: The backup flow exports supported wallet material and creates a separate encrypted file for each eligible wallet. Restore all-wallet backups one file at a time.

scope.label: Electrum and aezeed
scope.detail: These recovery formats are excluded from iCloud backup in this release. Retain their original recovery material and any required password or seed extension.

scope.label: Recently Deleted wallets
scope.detail: The all-wallet backup flow uses active wallets and excludes Recently Deleted wallets. A successful backup of one wallet does not establish that another was saved.

features.limitations: Backup availability depends on the wallet type, app version and iCloud Drive access. This page describes Oath 5.0.2 (104).
steps: Use the Apple Account that will hold the backup, enable iCloud Drive and check available storage. Open Settings → Backup in Oath.
Start Back Up All Wallets and choose a strong password of at least eight characters. Keep it somewhere you can reach without this phone.
Keep Oath open while it prepares the files. Review each wallet’s status and resolve failed or unavailable uploads before relying on the backup.

questions.q: How does Oath encrypt the backup?
questions.a: The reviewed release uses AES-256-GCM. A password-derived key uses PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 with 600,000 rounds and a fresh salt. A strong, recoverable password remains essential.

questions.q: Is this the same as an iPhone device backup?
questions.a: No. This feature creates Oath encrypted wallet files in iCloud Drive. Do not assume an ordinary device backup or Apple Account sign-in replaces an Oath backup file and its password.

questions.q: What if I forget the backup password?
questions.a: Oath cannot reset it or decrypt the old file with a new password. If the wallet is still accessible, create a new backup with a password you can retain. Keep independent recovery material, including any required passphrase.

questions.q: Does “uploading” mean my wallet is backed up?
questions.a: No. Wait for completion for the relevant wallet. Account, storage or network problems can leave an upload pending or failed.

features.name: Connect to dApps with WalletConnect
features.summary: Use WalletConnect with Oath on iPhone. Review the dApp, wallet, networks and permissions, then approve supported requests individually.

scope.label: Compatible EVM requests
scope.detail: Supported mainnet EVM connections allow the signing and transaction requests implemented in Oath. Arc connections are not supported in this release.

scope.label: Other supported networks
scope.detail: Oath supports compatible requests for Bitcoin, Solana, THORChain, XRP Ledger, Stellar, NEAR, Sui, Polkadot, TRON and Gram/TON. Available actions differ by network and dApp.

scope.label: dApp and protocol limits
scope.detail: The dApp must offer a compatible mobile WalletConnect connection. WalletConnect is separate from TON Connect and browser-extension-only connections. Unsupported required methods or networks can prevent a session.

features.limitations: A network in your portfolio does not guarantee every dApp or signing method works. The released app checks the requested network and method before proceeding.
steps: Open the intended website and choose WalletConnect. On another screen, scan the QR with Oath; on the same device, use the Oath link offered by the dApp.
Unlock Oath if asked. Check the website, wallet, networks and requested permissions before connecting. Reject a proposal you cannot explain.
Return to the dApp, then inspect each signature or transaction in Oath. Check the network, destination, amount and fee where applicable.

questions.q: Does connecting share my recovery phrase?
questions.a: No. A connection shares the approved public accounts and permits supported requests. Never enter recovery words or private keys into a dApp, and never publish a WalletConnect pairing QR or URI.

questions.q: Why can a connection be rejected?
questions.a: The proposal may be expired, or require a network, method or account the installed app cannot support. Read the message in Oath and start a fresh connection from the intended dApp if needed.

questions.q: Is connecting the same as approving a token allowance?
questions.a: No. Session approval and on-chain token access are separate. Review each request, and use the token-access tools to inspect supported allowances.

questions.q: Can every Oath network use every dApp?
questions.a: No. Compatibility depends on the network, wallet account and action requested by the dApp. Follow the relevant network guide and the options shown in your installed app.

features.name: Create and import recovery formats
features.summary: Create a new BIP39 wallet or import supported BIP39, Electrum and aezeed recovery material. Validation and signing happen on the device. Electrum and aezeed imports are Bitcoin-only and need manual recovery backups.

features.name: 57 app localizations
features.summary: Oath is available in 57 app localizations, with right-to-left layouts, local number formats and BIP39 word lists.

features.name: Open source, with a documented review scope
features.summary: The full source code is public on GitHub at https://github.com/OathWallet/oath-wallet. The published release includes its security model, verification record and reporting policy. Public source is available for review; it does not establish an independent audit or a verified match to the App Store binary.

features.name: Bitcoin address options
features.summary: Compatible Bitcoin wallets support Taproot, Native SegWit, nested SegWit and Legacy, depending on the imported material. Capabilities vary by network. Oath 5.0.2 does not support Silent Payments receiving or discovery; see the Silent Payments guide before relying on that feature.

features.name: Your display currency
features.summary: Choose from the app’s supported display currencies. Values are estimates based on available exchange-rate data.

features.name: Available market prices
features.summary: See available price quotes for supported assets. Quotes can be delayed or unavailable; displayed fiat values are estimates.

faq.q: How do I create a wallet?
faq.a: Open Oath and tap “Create a new wallet”. Your keys are generated on your iPhone, then you’ll back up your recovery phrase. Creating a local wallet needs no Oath account or email.

faq.q: Can I import a wallet from another app?
faq.a: Yes. Choose Import wallet and use the original BIP39, Electrum or aezeed format with any required passphrase. Electrum and aezeed restore supported Bitcoin accounts. Private keys use a separate import with the matching network. Compare a known public address before moving funds.

faq.q: Can I create my own recovery phrase with dice?
faq.a: The 5.0.2 source creates standard wallets with a 12-word BIP39 phrase. The earlier dice, coin-flip and typed-digit creation controls are not included in this release.

faq.q: What if I lose my iPhone?
faq.a: Install Oath on a compatible iPhone or iPad and use the correct recovery phrase and any extra passphrase, or an existing encrypted iCloud backup with its backup password. Your funds live on the blockchain, not on your phone.

faq.q: Can Oath recover my recovery phrase?
faq.a: No. Recovery material is protected locally in the app, not held by Oath support. Keep your own recovery backup; support cannot replace missing words, keys or passwords.

faq.q: How does backup password restore work?
faq.a: Eligible iCloud backups need both the .oathbackup file and the separate password used to encrypt it. The app passcode or Apple Account access alone cannot decrypt it. Electrum and aezeed wallets need manual recovery material in 5.0.2.

faq.q: Is a backup password a replacement for my recovery phrase?
faq.a: Eligible iCloud backups need both the .oathbackup file and the separate password used to encrypt it. The app passcode or Apple Account access alone cannot decrypt it. Electrum and aezeed wallets need manual recovery material in 5.0.2.
Transactions confirm when the network includes them. Busy networks take longer. You can see the status and the fee you paid in the transaction details.
Fees go to the network, not to Oath. A network-fee estimate is shown before you confirm; the final fee can depend on the network and transaction.

faq.q: Which address type should I use for Bitcoin?
faq.a: Native SegWit (bc1q) and Taproot (bc1p) are efficient Bitcoin address options. The best choice depends on sender compatibility and how your coins will be spent. Nested SegWit and Legacy are also available where supported by the imported material. Silent Payments receiving and discovery are not supported in 5.0.2.

faq.q: Someone from “Oath support” asked for my phrase.
faq.a: That is a scam. Oath will never ask for your recovery phrase, private key or passkey. Don’t reply, and forward the message to care@oathwallet.org.

Yes. The full source is published on GitHub at github.com/OathWallet/oath-wallet, with a current security model, release verification record and security policy. Public source does not establish an independent audit or a verified match to the App Store binary.
A tool that shows discovered token approvals on supported EVM networks. Revoke a supported permission with an on-chain transaction; a network fee applies.

faq.q: Does revoking an approval cost a fee?
faq.a: Yes, a small network fee, because revoking is an on-chain transaction. Oath shows it before you confirm.

faq.q: What is a self-custody crypto wallet?
faq.a: A self-custody, or non-custodial, wallet lets you authorize transactions with your wallet’s private keys. The crypto remains recorded on its blockchain. Your wallet helps you manage the credentials and addresses used to access it. Keeping a usable recovery method is your responsibility.

faq.q: How is a wallet different from an exchange account?
faq.a: With a custodial exchange account, the provider controls the withdrawal keys. With self-custody, you manage the signing credentials. This removes reliance on an exchange to approve a withdrawal, but it also means a forgotten recovery phrase, a malicious approval or a mistaken transfer can cause permanent loss.

faq.q: Can I use Oath for Bitcoin and other crypto on iPhone?
faq.a: Oath Wallet is available for iPhone and iPad. Choose the asset and network in the app before sharing a receiving address. A matching coin name or address format does not mean two networks are interchangeable. Available actions depend on your app version, network and wallet type.

faq.q: What happens if I lose my phone?
faq.a: Recovery depends on the backup you prepared before the loss. A recovery phrase may also require its separate BIP-39 passphrase. Oath’s optional iCloud recovery needs the encrypted backup and the backup password. Check your recovery method before relying on it, and never share recovery words with support.

faq.q: Is Oath free, and why do transfers have fees?
faq.a: Oath is free to download from the App Store. Blockchain transfers can require network fees, account reserves or activation costs. These vary by network and conditions. Review the asset, destination, network and fee before confirming; an on-chain transfer generally cannot be reversed.
